papers.title: Effects of sequence splitting and negative-set selection on antimicrobial peptide prediction
papers.abstract: Sequence partitioning and negative-set selection determine the prediction problem posed by an antimicrobial peptide (AMP) benchmark. We quantified their effects using a DRAMP 5.0 audit, controlled comparisons with frozen ESM-2 classifiers and additional benchmark configurations. On DRAMP, random splitting increased Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) from 0.718 under cluster-disjoint splitting to 0.932. This difference of 0.214 exceeded the gains from the architectural additions tested, and 75.6% of randomly assigned test sequences shared a homology cluster with training sequences. Across three additional dataset configurations, random-minus-cluster MCC differences ranged from -0.04634 to +0.05682, showing that the magnitude and direction of the split effect depended on benchmark composition. With the fitted classifiers and APD6 positives held fixed, replacing DRAMP test negatives with external hard negatives reduced the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.9833 to 0.9018 (paired difference 0.08149, bootstrap 95% CI 0.07196 to 0.09181). These comparisons quantify substantial sensitivity to evaluation design and show why split effects require assessment within each benchmark. AMPBenchAudit provides the audited records, split assignments and evaluation code needed to examine this sensitivity and interpret model comparisons under explicit test conditions.

papers.title: Zero-shot virtual knock-out rankings do not recover causal genes from observational single-cell data
papers.abstract: Background: Virtual knock-out methods rank genes by the change predicted after deleting one gene in silico and nominate targets without perturbation data. That use assumes the ranking reflects the causal consequence of removal; we tested it for three zero-shot methods in four configurations under one criterion. Results: We compared scTenifoldKnk (R and Python), CellOracle and Geneformer on 438 real, 3,585 synthetic and 330 DepMap knock-outs. Top-20 lists of different knock-outs overlapped by a median of 12 to 14 of 20, against 0.08 by chance. Displacement followed out-degree (R^2 = 0.825; 0.852 with six further features). Decoupling causal effect from topology left criterion value and grade unchanged (36 of 36 RED). For scTenifoldKnk, the ranking showed no evidence of recovery above chance where causal genes were planted (AUROC 0.538 and 0.528 in the two constructions). CellOracle's displacement showed no detectable relation to the data-built network (rho = -0.212, P = 0.556). Geneformer's shift tracked token coverage inconsistently (+0.41, +0.40, -0.27). Against DepMap essentiality, scTenifoldKnk's Python implementation (scTenifoldpy 0.5.1) reached AUROC 0.459 (95% CI 0.357-0.566), not distinguishable from chance; detection rate reached 0.588 (95% CI 0.497-0.677). Conclusions: For scTenifoldKnk and CellOracle, the ranking reports network properties, not the causal consequence of removal. No measured structural feature accounted for more than a small fraction of Geneformer's shift. Detection rate, needing no network, gained +0.129 (95% CI 0.0017-0.2543; 97.6% of resamples positive) over the tool.

papers.title: Integrating CRISPRi perturbation responses and transcription-factor binding priors for regulatory network inference in triple-negative breast cancer
papers.abstract: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) represents an aggressive breast cancer subtype that lacks actionable cell-surface receptors, restricting frontline systemic management to cytotoxic chemotherapy. While recent functional epigenomics shows that TNBC progression is governed by non-coding regulatory remodeling at distal super-enhancers, conventional Gene Regulatory Network (GRN) inference methods rely on observational transcriptomic co-expression, which suffers from technical dropouts and confounding correlations that inflate false discoveries (>30%). Here, we present an interventional network inference framework that integrates large-scale single-cell CRISPR-interference perturbation sequencing (Perturb-seq; GSE224986, 95,678 cells across 11,975 sgRNAs) with ENCODE Factorbook ChIP-seq physical transcription factor binding priors across 819 somatic mutation-associated enhancer loci in human TNBC (MDA-MB-231). Our pipeline reconstructed a tripartite network yielding 5,935 physical TF-enhancer edges, 383,757 functional enhancer-gene edges, and 542,760 unique TF-target gene functional pairs across 372 active enhancers. Topological centrality prioritized master transcriptional drivers governing TNBC oncogenic signaling, including CTCF, POLR2A, EP300, JUND, MYC, and FOS, which regulate Hallmark programs for Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (p = 1.2 x 10-9) and cell cycle progression. Explainable machine learning (SHAP TreeExplainer) revealed non-linear, thresholded transactivation dynamics for AP-1 and MYC. Quantitative benchmarking against held-out CRISPRi ground truth demonstrated strong discriminatory accuracy (AUROC = 0.8999, AUPRC = 0.8745, Precision = 90.13%, FDR = 9.87%), substantially outperforming GENIE3 (AUPRC = 0.6323, FDR = 35.73%) and co-expression correlation (AUPRC = 0.6814). In silico-simulated driver feature silencing correlated with experimental responses (R2 = 0.473, p < 10-122), and master driver signatures significantly stratified overall survival in the METABRIC (n = 320) and TCGA-BRCA (n = 160; p [≤] 0.019) cohorts. Finally, in silico perturbation modeling indicated that multi-target epigenetic combinations achieved 93% topological disruption of oncogenic regulatory connectivity, nominating prioritized candidate circuits for experimental validation.

papers.title: TrailMix: Mixture Proportion and Placement Estimation of Ancient Hominin mtDNA Samples using a Pangenomic Reference
papers.abstract: Hominin mitochondrial DNA extracted from sediments or ancient environments is sometimes a mixture of multiple contributing sources. Researchers must subsequently computationally identify from which mitochondrial lineages the DNA sequences comes (e.g. Denisovan vs. modern human superhaplogroup) and ideally, quantify their abundance. Bioinformatics approaches described in the literature to achieve this involve in-house scripts or heuristics applied to tools designed for other datasets. However, such approaches have neither been fully tested nor do they provide credible intervals on model parameters. To address this, we introduce TrailMix, a C++ program for estimating contributing mixture proportions as well as individual source placements on the hominin mitochondrial tree for ancient environmental DNA. Using a pangenome reference graph to mitigate reference-related bias, TrailMix works well to accurately deconvolve mixtures of multiple mitochondrial lineages and place each contributor within its respective phylogenetic context. Crucially, it allows users to place minor contributing sources on the tree even on ancestral nodes without needing to reach consensus in the presence of multiple sources. TrailMix is part of the vgan suite of tools and is available at https://github.com/grenaud/vgan.

papers.title: deeprok: highly accurate prokaryotic gene prediction through deep learning and overlap-aware decoding
papers.abstract: Prokaryotic gene prediction is often considered solved, yet widely used tools still disagree on many genes, chiefly short genes and translation starts. We present deeprok, an ab initio prokaryotic gene prediction method that combines a base-level neural network with an overlap-aware decoder, and refines start-site predictions with a self-trained neural ranker. On four curated genomes distant from its training data, deeprok made 10-18% fewer exact-match errors than Prodigal and GeneMarkS-2, and on 2,925 experimentally verified starts it made 21-41% fewer start errors. Furthermore, deeprok's base-level architecture reveals lineage-specific translation initiation signals. These results show that per-base deep learning combined with overlap-aware decoding can improve prokaryotic gene prediction, especially for resolving translation starts.

papers.title: Multiscale superinformation reveals structured organization of genomic sequence features
papers.abstract: Genomic sequence organization varies across spatial scales, but sequence complexity measures are often evaluated at a single resolution. Superinformation (SI), introduced by Bose and Chouhan, measures heterogeneity in local sequence entropy by taking the entropy of the distribution of block-level Shannon entropy values. We characterize SI across 14 Sequence Ontology-defined genomic feature classes in seven species and seven block sizes from 20 to 200 bp. SI profiles were non-increasing for 72 of 86 evaluable species-feature combinations, although this pattern was not universal. Observed SI generally exceeded both a block-count-controlled random null and a species-level GC-controlled null. Associations with mononucleotide entropy, dinucleotide entropy, and GC content were modest, with no individual descriptor explaining more than 10.4% of the observed variation. For the 13 complete feature-level profiles used in geometric analysis, the first two principal components explained 97.859% of the variance, and hierarchical clustering grouped features with similar SI trajectories. We also summarize the profiles using the Characteristic Information Scale and Information Persistence Score. These analyses extend the original superinformation framework to a comparative, multiscale analysis of genomic feature heterogeneity while keeping the interpretation of SI limited to the sequence properties measured here.

papers.title: Genomic foundation models and complementary variant-scoring strategies in LGMD-associated genes: architecture, adaptation, and sequence context
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models learn representations from DNA sequence, although their usefulness for variant classification depends on the architecture and downstream evaluation procedure. We compared six genomic foundation models using 6,960 ClinVar single-nucleotide variants from ten limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD)-associated genes, with 4,866 variants assigned to training and 2,094 to held-out testing. The analyses included frozen alternate-minus-reference embeddings at 101, 201 and 501 bp, supervised adaptation at 101 bp, and gene-held-out downstream classifier training. GPN-Star V100 and AlphaGenome Atlas AVI were evaluated separately using their native scores. At 101 bp, frozen Evo2 achieved the highest discrimination among the six foundation models (MCC 0.644; AUROC 0.879; AUPRC 0.818). Supervised adaptation increased MCC for three architectures and reduced it for the remaining three. Extending sequence context to 501 bp improved all three primary metrics in five of six frozen architectures, with Evo2 reaching an MCC of 0.864, AUROC of 0.964 and AUPRC of 0.952. Evo2 also led the frozen gene-held-out readouts (pooled MCC 0.641; AUROC 0.852; AUPRC 0.789). GPN-Star V100 and AVI achieved MCC values of 0.929 and 0.938, respectively, using distinct biological inputs and scoring procedures. The number of variants misclassified across all evaluated configurations decreased from five under the original 101-bp readouts to one after including longer contexts and native scores. An exploratory HGVS-category control identified substantial annotation-associated structure in the benchmark labels. The findings characterize classification performance against aggregate ClinVar labels within LGMD-associated genes. Disease-specific pathogenicity and clinical diagnostic utility remain untested.

papers.title: Deciphering state bridges via a single-cell large language model
papers.abstract: Large-scale single-cell transcriptomic data provide a new avenue for precision medicine by uncovering cellular heterogeneity. However, systematic comparison of remodeling patterns across various biological states remains unavailable. Here, we first developed a computational framework based on a foundation model of single cell biology, Universal Cell Embedding (UCE), to harmonize annotations comprising 36 cell types. Based on an integrated dataset of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with 8,789 human samples comprising more than 59 million cells or nuclei across 614 biological states, we then embedded each state with a 36-dimensional vector in a unified space of cell-composition change and further deciphered states bridges by analyzing the relationships among the 614 state vectors. As a result, 22,161 significant bridges (P < 0.05) between the 614 states were revealed. Moreover, we successfully identified a number of well-known bridges such as bridge between Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (P = 2.21e-15), suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed framework. More importantly, we uncovered a number of new bridges. Furthermore, analyses of the number of changed cell types (NCC) and Shannon entropy revealed heterogeneous and tissue-dependent patterns of cellular composition remodeling. This study provides a new strategy for identifying disease associations and potential therapeutic relationships by deciphering bridges between biological states from scRNA-seq landscape.

papers.title: How predictable is an individual's DNA methylation?
papers.abstract: DNA methylation is largely shared among individuals of the same cell type, yet at specific genomic sites it differs substantially between individuals. Methods that predict methylation are usually evaluated by their accuracy over all sites. Because methylation at most sites is shared, this accuracy cannot show whether a method predicts an individual's methylation where individuals differ. We present individual-level methylation prediction at sites where individuals differ as a new challenge. Given the reference genome sequence, the methylation of other individuals of the same cell type, and measurements at some sites of a target individual, but not the individual's genotype, the task is to predict the target individual's methylation class (unmethylated, intermediate, or methylated) at the remaining sites. We evaluate predictions separately at sites with low and high variation across individuals. We compare four approaches: the average of other individuals, a sequence model (the DNA language model Nucleotide Transformer) fine-tuned on other individuals' methylation, the same model further fine-tuned on the target individual's measurements, and a local class-average approach using the target individual's nearby training-site class labels. Across 32 individuals from six human cell types, the average of other individuals matched or slightly exceeded both sequence models at sites with low variation among individuals. At the most variable sites, the average of other individuals performed worse than a random predictor that assigns classes at the observed class frequencies, whereas both sequence models performed substantially better than the average. Both sequence models also achieved higher mean weighted F1 than the local class-average approach. Fine-tuning on the target individual's measurements improved predictions more inside regions where other individuals show bimodal methylation (a mix of methylated and unmethylated DNA molecules within one sample) than outside them. Among the most variable sites, it also improved predictions at CpG islands for 25 of the 32 individuals. We conclude that individual-level methylation prediction is a distinct problem that is particularly challenging at sites where individuals differ, and that the benefit of an individual's own measurements is concentrated in genomic contexts identifiable from other individuals' methylation and genomic annotations.

papers.title: Transpiling reproducibility: Multi-language implementation for the St. Nicolas House Analysis algorithm using Fusion
papers.abstract: The integration of tools written in different programming languages is common in bioinformatics pipelines. When extending these tools, developers are required to either manually port the code or use wrapper libraries, which incurs a substantial "translation tax" on developer time. Transpilers have emerged as a potential solution, enabling the generation of algorithm implementations in multiple languages from a single source code base. However, it remains essential to establish whether transpiled code preserves both functional correctness and stochastic reproducibility across language ecosystems. In this case study, we investigated whether the Fusion language and its fut transpiler could produce functionally identical, stochastically reproducible, and high-performing code for the St. Nicolas House Analysis (SNHA) algorithm across multiple target languages. The SNHA algorithm was implemented once in Fusion and transpiled to nine target programming languages. The generated code was evaluated against reference R, Python, and Julia implementations using the clinical birthwt dataset and a 26-variable synthetic benchmark dataset evaluated over 1,000 bootstrap iterations. All nine transpiled outputs produced identical network structures to the original R implementation. With the deterministic Xorshift*64 pseudo-random number generator integrated into the algorithm, all languages generated identical bootstrapped datasets and adjacency matrices. Runtimes and memory usage spanned more than two orders of magnitude: the transpiled Python implementation achieved an 8.5-fold speedup and an 8.8-fold reduction in peak memory relative to reference Python, while compiled targets (C, C++) achieved speedups exceeding 160-fold and memory reductions up to 36-fold. These findings demonstrate that modern transpilers can eliminate cross-ecosystem translation tax while guaranteeing cross-language reproducibility in computational biology.

papers.title: Plasma electrolyte changes can modulate post-repolarisation refractoriness in the human atrium
papers.abstract: Changes in plasma Na+, K+ and Ca2+ levels are common in patients with chronic kidney disease or gastrointestinal disorders, or in those taking certain medications, and may promote atrial fibrillation or impair drug-induced cardioversion. Post-repolarisation refractoriness (PRR) is an established mechanism by which antiarrhythmic drugs suppress tachyarrhythmias. We investigated how changes in extracellular Na+, K+ and Ca2+ concentrations ([Na+]o, [K+]o, [Ca2+]o) modulate ionic currents and PRR in healthy and fibrotic human atrial tissue. We used a multi-scale computational framework comprising an isolated atrial myocyte, a one-dimensional atrial tissue strand, and a virtual cohort of 14 left atrial digital twins, combined with Gaussian process emulators and variance-based global sensitivity analysis. Changes in [K+]o strongly modulated PRR by altering the inward rectifier K+ current (IK1), shifting the resting potential and thereby regulating Na+-current availability. In contrast, [Na+]o had only a weak effect on PRR, mediated primarily through the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and [Ca2+]o had a negligible effect. Tissue PRR was more sensitive to electrolyte changes than myocyte PRR, reflecting electrolyte-dependent alterations in the safety factor for action potential propagation. Changes in [K+]o also substantially affected arrhythmia vulnerability, increasing inducibility and prolonging rhythm disturbances. We conclude that extracellular K+ is the principal plasma electrolyte determinant of atrial PRR and arrhythmia burden, acting primarily through IK1. Monitoring and maintaining serum K+ within the normal range may be important for managing atrial arrhythmia risk.

papers.title: Identification of eukaryotes as a bycatch in global microbiome data
papers.abstract: Eukaryotes shape microbiomes as macroscopic hosts, microscopic community members, and food sources, yet the diversity and ecological significance of microbial eukaryotes remain poorly resolved. Here, we present metaEukaryome, an organelle genome-centered framework for detection of eukaryotes in metagenomic data that leverages mitochondrial and plastid sequences as robust signatures of presence. Applying metaEukaryome to 75,727 metagenomic samples collected across the globe reveals strong environment-specific patterns in the prevalence of detected eukaryotes. Integrating eukaryotic and prokaryotic profiles further reveals recurrent cross-domain co-occurrence and symbiosis in the human gut. In particular, Blastocystis is associated with metabolically reduced, uncultured bacterial clades, including Candidatus Borkfalkia and CAG-345, whose DNA and RNA are detected in a Blastocystis culture previously reported as axenic. Their complementary metabolic repertoires further support a candidate symbiotic relationship. These findings imply that more novel (endo-)symbionts of gut protists can be discovered by reanalysing existing data.

papers.title: The IGVF Data Portal: a repository for insights into genome function
papers.abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) Consortium has utilized a wide variety of assays and computational methods to study how genomic variation impacts function. To support the collaborative efforts of labs within IGVF, and to share the results of these efforts, the IGVF Data Administration and Coordination Center (DACC) has developed a data portal (https://data.igvf.org/) that serves as the repository for all results from the IGVF Consortium and as the source of results that have been integrated into the IGVF knowledge graph. Data generated by the IGVF Consortium, which has reached over 240 terabytes as of November 2026, can be publicly accessed via web browser, or programmatically via API, as well as via agentic tools. Here, we provide a summary of the available IGVF data and an overview of the design of the IGVF Data Portal.

papers.title: Unsupervised tensor integration of hippocampal and colonic multi-omics reveals enteric neural signatures in cognitive aging
papers.abstract: Background: Molecular changes in peripheral tissues may provide insights into cognitive aging, but identifying relevant genes without using behavioral outcomes for feature selection remains challenging. Results: We applied tensor decomposition-based unsupervised feature extraction to publicly available hippocampal and colonic transcriptomic and promoter DNA methylation profiles from mice across five age groups. A tensor comprising tissue, molecular modality, age group, biological replicate, and gene dimensions was constructed using 16,080 shared genes. Higher-order singular value decomposition identified a component with a monotonic age pattern, shared tissue contributions, and opposing transcriptomic and methylation contributions. This component yielded 1,577 selected genes without using cognitive scores for feature selection. The corresponding colonic methylation score correlated with overall cognition (r=0.589; Benjamini--Hochberg-adjusted P=9.87 x10-7), although no significant associations remained after age adjustment. The selected genes were enriched for enteric neuronal and glial markers derived from a published single-cell atlas, with 5.10-fold and 4.65-fold enrichment, respectively. Comparison with the broadest available Boruta-selected gene set identified only 64 overlapping genes, leaving 1,513 genes selected exclusively by the tensor approach in this comparison. These remaining genes retained significant enrichment for synaptic processes and enteric neuronal and glial signatures using library-specific backgrounds. Conclusions: Unsupervised tensor integration recovered an aging-associated relationship between colonic methylation and cognition while identifying a largely distinct set of functionally coherent candidate genes. These findings complement supervised feature selection and provide candidates for investigating enteric neural involvement in cognitive aging, without establishing an age-independent association or a causal gut-to-brain mechanism.

papers.title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
papers.abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) consortium is systematically characterizing how genomic variation influences regulatory elements, gene expression, and human phenotypes through thousands of experimental mapping and perturbation datasets alongside predictive models. To synthesize these diverse results into quantitative relationships and situate them within established biological knowledge, we developed the IGVF Catalog, a large-scale knowledge graph. Implemented in ArangoDB using schema-validated JSON records. Version 1.3 encompasses nearly 3 billion nodes across 14 entity types (including variants, coding variants, genomic elements, genes, transcripts, proteins, pathways, and ontology graphs for biosamples and phenotypes) connected by more than 8.6 billion edges across 31 relationship types. Edges encode statistical significance, effect sizes, source provenance, and biological context via ontology-linked hyperedges. The Catalog integrates 657 IGVF datasets spanning non-coding reporter and CRISPR perturbation screens (MPRA, STARR-seq, Perturb-seq), coding variant assays (VAMP-seq, SGE, MAVE, DUAL-IPA), and predictive models (scE2G, SEMVAR, cV2F, TLAND, and BlueSTARR), unified with extensive public context including GENCODE annotations, FAVOR and dbSNP variants, TopLD linkage disequilibrium, GWAS, QTLs, and protein interactions. Users can interrogate the Catalog through a web portal (https://igvf.catalog.org) Python and R clients, an OpenAPI-documented API featuring 86 endpoints supporting identifier and genomic-region queries, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling agent-assisted querying with large language models. We demonstrate the Catalog's utility for mechanistic interpretation across three case studies: resolving a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant (rs11257655) regulating CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus, distinguishing coding (GCKR rs1260326) and regulatory (HNF1A rs1169289) mechanisms for liver traits, and linking vascular CRISPRi-perturbed elements to CDKN2A/CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease. Updated quarterly with open data and software, the IGVF Catalog provides a scalable resource for variant-to-function discovery.

papers.title: SpliceVarMech: A causal generative framework for mechanistic interpretation of non-canonical splicing variants
papers.abstract: Non-canonical splicing variants occur beyond the conserved dinucleotides flanking splice junctions and are difficult to interpret because disruption scores alone do not explain splice outcomes or quantify uncertainty. We have developed SpliceVarMech, a causal generative framework in which a dual-stream encoder compares the wild-type and mutant sequences and conditional discrete sequence diffusion generates candidate splice outcomes. We then apply Bayesian causal inference to estimate posterior disruption probabilities with 95% credible intervals. The framework reports the predicted splice mechanism together with sequence attribution maps and an exploratory mapping to clinical evidence labels. On a gold-standard cohort of experimentally validated variants from male infertility genes, Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation on 31 variants yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 1.000. We benchmarked 16 individual splice prediction tools on the same cohort, where the highest-performing tool, SpliceAI, achieved 0.619 on its 30 scored variants. Ablation experiments showed that removing individual components reduced discrimination, and a separate evaluation on 54 variants supported the contribution of fine-tuning. In a cross-domain assessment, fine-tuning on BRCA1 saturation genome editing data increased discrimination from 0.722 to 0.840 on 203 held-out variants without architectural modification. We assessed in-sample calibration, and held-out validation remains necessary. These results support further evaluation of paired-sequence generative modeling and Bayesian inference for mechanistic interpretation of splicing variants across disease contexts.

papers.title: gutenTAG: A MALDI-IHC processing and quality control tool
papers.abstract: Coupling of immunohistochemistry with MALDI mass spectroscopy (MALDI-IHC) enables targeted spatial analysis of proteins through the use of photocleavable mass tags. Upwards of 100 proteins can be imaged in a single run due to the high multiplexing power of this technology. Coupled with mass shifts in MALDI-IHC data, this scalability creates a challenge for users, as there are currently no dedicated software tools for MALDI-IHC data processing. Here we introduce gutenTAG, an open-source processing and quality control tool specifically designed for MALDI-IHC. gutenTAG uses a novel strategy based on grouping clusters of m/z bins originating from the same molecular species into single entities termed metapeaks. This strategy is robust to mass shift, generating ion images that capture the full signal of peaks corresponding to each mass tag while minimizing noise. Furthermore, we show that the metapeak strategy can be adapted to alternative open-source tools to facilitate their use in targeted imaging applications.

papers.title: SCOPE: Gaussian-regularized graph learning for enzyme catalytic residue prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of catalytic residues is central to understanding enzyme mechanisms and engineering biocatalysts, yet annotation remains challenging because experimentally validated sites are sparse. Here, we present SCOPE, a graph learning framework for catalytic residue prediction that integrates evolutionary, physicochemical, and three-dimensional structural information at the residue level. SCOPE represents enzymes as residue-level structural graphs and incorporates a Gaussian auxiliary training objective that aggregates structure-aware representations along sequence order. Evaluations across five benchmark datasets, CATH family-disjoint retraining and the external CataloDB benchmark assess predictive performance and generalization. Structural analyses associate complete catalytic-residue recovery with compact active-site arrangements. We further validated SCOPE prospectively across four enzymes using site-directed mutagenesis and activity assays, confirming multiple predicted residues as functionally important. These results support SCOPE as a framework for catalytic residue annotation and prioritizing functional sites for experimental investigation.

papers.title: Dependence-Aware Conformal Prediction for 3D Uncertainty Quantification in Molecular Docking
papers.abstract: Molecular docking plays a critical role in drug discovery by predicting three-dimensional (3D) binding poses of small molecules within proteins. However, docking predictions can contain substantial positional errors, making reliable uncertainty quantification essential. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, yet constructing compact 3D prediction regions with reliable joint coverage remains challenging due to heterogeneous atomic errors, dependence among spatial coordinates, and distribution shifts. We develop a dependence-aware CP framework for molecular docking that leverages a shared graph neural network (GNN) to estimate adaptive, asymmetric uncertainty intervals using local atomic and global molecular information. Copula-based joint calibration accounts for dependence among coordinate-wise nonconformity scores to construct compact 3D prediction boxes. We further introduce density ratio estimation (DRE) to adapt calibration under distribution shift. Experiments across three docking methods demonstrate that our approach reduces median prediction-box volumes by 37.40%, 95.00%, and 39.16% for AutoDock Vina, Protenix, and MedusaGraph, respectively, compared with a state-of-the-art CP baseline, while achieving empirical joint coverage close to the 90% target. Under the Molecular Group Split and controlled distribution shifts, DRE further reduces coverage deviations, highlighting the potential of dependence-aware and shift-adaptive calibration for reliable 3D molecular docking uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: siGMA: Modeling Label Noise and Heterogeneity in siRNA Efficacy Prediction
papers.abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) have emerged as a powerful class of therapeutics, yet identifying viable candidates remains costly and labour-intensive given the vast combination space that must be screened. This challenge is compounded by the need for chemical modifications, which are essential to mitigate off-target effects and enhance serum stability but frequently come at the expense of baseline knockdown efficacy. As a result, siRNA design requires careful, iterative optimization, further expanding the experimental burden and rendering exhaustive screening impractical. Computational prediction offers a compelling alternative, enabling rapid, low-cost identification of promising candidates prior to wet-lab validation. In this work we present siGMA, a heteroscedastic multimodal predictive model that integrates sequence, chemical, structural, and experimental information to predict the silencing efficacy of chemically modified siRNAs. Modelling in this domain is constrained by two principal obstacles: the scarcity of experimental data and the substantial noise arising from protocol heterogeneity across publicly available datasets. We therefore propose a model that quantifies predictive uncertainty rather than issuing confident mispredictions. We calibrated the model against such noise using a combined aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty prediction. The resulting model yielded well-calibrated estimates of predictive variability on held-out folds across datasets and outperformed current state-of-the-art approaches across noisy cross-dataset conditions, including previously unseen chemical modifications and target sequences. This demonstrates our model's ability to rank better than the baselines while rendering the noise ceiling measurable. This provides a scalable framework that could accelerate the therapeutic siRNA development pipeline while reducing the need for exhaustive empirical screening.

papers.title: A2Holo: Dual-Stream Flow Matching of 3D Structure and a Protein Language Model for Conformational Transition Prediction
papers.abstract: Modelling a ligand-bound holo conformation from a ligand-free apo conformation is essential in structure-based drug discovery. We present A2Holo, which casts apo-to-holo prediction as flow matching between two experimental structures rather than generation from noise. It transplants the dual-stream joint attention of in-context image generation to residue-aligned protein language model embeddings and structure. Without ligand conditioning or stochastic sampling, A2Holo's single deterministic trajectory reaches a median C RMSD of 0.809 [A] on the D3PM benchmark, the lowest among existing methods. Its TM-score exceeds even the best of 10 samples from every stochastic baseline on at least 144 of 150 pairs. Beyond performance, we directly measure the transplanted multimodal mechanism itself. Because sequence and structure are residue-aligned, its joint attention can be measured at residue resolution and tested for reproducibility across independently trained model variants. Within the structure stream, the attention a residue receives recovers moving residues better than the attention it emits, and this asymmetry is learned. A2Holo demonstrates a successful multimodal transplant from in-context image generation to protein conformational change, with strong deterministic apo-to-holo prediction. It also provides a quantitative account of how that mechanism organises residue-aligned sequence and structure around the residues that move.

papers.title: Large populations from few founders: founder-aware likelihoods for inferring cell proliferation rates
papers.abstract: Gaussian approximations to demographic noise are usually justified by large numbers of cells. In populations described by branching processes, however, a large population descended from few founders is not approximately Gaussian. A culture grown from few cells can contain thousands of cells yet retain large, skewed variation from its earliest divisions, deaths, and phenotypic switches. A random establishment amplitude, the limit of the population size divided by its exponential growth factor, summarizes this variation. We propose a founder-aware likelihood for cell cultures observed at an endpoint. Given the establishment amplitude, it approximates the remaining demographic fluctuations by a Gaussian distribution and then averages over the distribution of the amplitude. Its conditional Gaussian approximation requires a large population rather than many founders, and the likelihood approaches a single Gaussian distribution as the founder count grows. We compare it with a population Gaussian likelihood developed for many-founder cultures, using a pure-birth (Yule) process, whose cell-count distribution is known exactly, and exact simulations of a two-type process with division, death, and reversible switching. With one founder per culture, the founder-aware likelihood estimates rates more accurately than the population Gaussian likelihood, and its confidence sets are longer but have coverage close to the nominal level. With 50 founders per culture, the two likelihoods perform comparably. Founder-aware likelihoods thus suit clonal and other few-founder experiments.

papers.title: Predicted templates improve the prediction of antibody-antigen structures by AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2
papers.abstract: Motivation: In spite of the much improved protein structure prediction methods, the success rate remains low for antibody-antigen complexes. While this can be improved by computationally demanding massive sampling, results are still much poorer than for most other types of protein-protein interactions. In principle, improvement can be achieved by using templates that are close enough to the native structure of the complex, but these are generally not available for antibody-antigen complexes. Results: We explore the use of templates, generated by the computationally inexpensive rigid body docking program PIPER. Applied to a leakage-free antibody-antigen benchmark set, standard AlphaFold 3 with 1000 random seeds yields acceptable or better models as the top predictions for 56.2% of complexes. Adding the PIPER generated templates in the unmasked version of AlphaFold 3 either increases the success rate to 63.4%, or reaches the same 56.2% success rate in about 200 runs. The template-based approach similarly improves antibody-antigen prediction by Boltz-2. This result demonstrates that the space explored by the ML based approach can be expanded by adding templates prepared by traditional docking, compensating for the lack of evolutionary relationship and the limited availability of training data. Availability and Implementation: The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/login.php) containing the PIPER program is free for non-commercial applications and the program is available by request (https://www.vajdalab.org/). All other study data are included in the article and/or supporting information.

papers.title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory metagenomes
papers.abstract: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific {chi}2-ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Performance for P. aeruginosa was more heterogeneous: long-read models performed well for amikacin, reaching 0.89 with PacBio and 0.88 with Nanopore, whereas Illumina performed substantially better for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, and levofloxacin, reaching accuracies of approximately 0.87, 0.77, and 0.70, respectively. Across most organism-antibiotic combinations, RF accuracy was numerically higher than the classification accuracies obtained with KARGA and ResFinder, which generally remained near 0.50. Increasing pathogen abundance from 5% to 10% and increasing the number of selected features from 2,500 to 5,000 generally produced modest improvements in classification accuracy, although the magnitude of improvement varied across organism-antibiotic combinations and sequencing platforms. Conclusions: Genome-wide k-mer machine learning can recover phenotype-associated antimicrobial resistance signals from simulated respiratory metagenomes, although performance depends strongly on the organism, antibiotic, and sequencing platform. These results represent a simulation-based proof of concept.

papers.title: NanoHIV-DR: a Nextflow workflow for consensus and read level HIV-1 drug resistance profiling from Oxford Nanopore sequencing
papers.abstract: Oxford Nanopore sequencing offers a rapid and portable approach for HIV-1 drug resistance (HIVDR) genotyping, but analysis of the resulting long-read data requires multiple bioinformatics steps and currently available nanopore workflows are limited. We developed NanoHIV-DR, a Nextflow-based workflow that streamlines the analysis of Oxford Nanopore sequencing data and generation of HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR processes raw POD5 files through basecalling, demultiplexing, host-read removal, quality filtering, read alignment and consensus generation, before identifying resistance-associated mutations and interpreting predicted drug susceptibility. The workflow provides two complementary approaches to HIVDR analysis: consensus-based resistance interpretation using Sierra and read-level detection of resistance-associated variants, enabling mutations below the consensus level to be identified and quantified. Outputs are integrated with clinical metadata to generate human-readable HIVDR reports. NanoHIV-DR provides a reproducible and accessible workflow for Nanopore-based HIVDR analysis with reduced bioinformatics expertise and manual processing for translating long-read sequencing data into interpretable resistance profiles.

papers.title: Machine Learning-based Transcriptomic Data Analysis of Long COVID Patients: Generating Hypotheses for Molecular Signatures
papers.abstract: Introduction: Long COVID (LC) remains a global public-health challenge, affecting an estimated 10-30% of COVID-19-survivors. Machine learning (ML) can help identify molecular features associated with LC. Human ion channels (HICs), that regulate immune-cell signaling and cellular homeostasis, may contribute to LC-associated processes and offer insights into relevant pathways and potential drug-repurposing candidates. Methodology: RNA-seq data from COVID-19-recovered and LC patients across six datasets were integrated, preprocessed, and corrected for batch effects. Supervised ML models were evaluated using leave-one-batch-out validation, with SHAP identifying features across validation folds. Functional enrichment, host-host and host-viral protein-protein interaction analyses were performed, followed by drug interaction analysis of potential HICs within the resulting interactome. Results: A support vector classifier with an RBF kernel achieved a mean-AUC of 0.664 across six validation folds. SHAP analysis of the three selected folds (AUC = 0.722, 0.836, and 0.817) identified 225, 153, and 241 genes, respectively. Functional enrichment highlighted pathways including histidine metabolism and TNF signaling. Among the 613 genes identified across these folds, 9 were HICs and 39 were immune signaling-related genes (ISGs), whose protein-protein interaction analysis revealed a pharmacologically relevant interactome. Furthermore, four HICs including CLCN3, KCNQ3, RYR1, and ZACN interacted with 30 approved drugs. Conclusion: ML-based analysis of integrated RNA-seq data identified HICs and ISGs associated with LC, while functional enrichment and PPI analyses provided insights into their potential biological relevance. Drug interaction analysis further highlighted candidate HIC-targeting drugs for future investigation in LC management. This computational framework provides preliminary, hypothesis-generating insights to guide future research.

papers.title: The Impact of Germ Layer Origin on the Ageing Transcriptome
papers.abstract: Ageing is accompanied by widespread changes in gene expression, yet whether these changes share any common organisation across groups of tissues remains unclear. Adult tissues arise from three embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm), so shared developmental lineage could influence how tissues age. Using bulk RNA-seq data from 24 GTEx tissues, we estimated age effects in each tissue with limma-voom and combined them within each germ layer by random-effects meta-analysis. Endoderm had the most significant age-associated genes (4,805), followed by mesoderm (4,520) and ectoderm (1,744), but this order reversed for genes with consistent effects across tissues of the same germ layer. These consistent genes were largely germ layer specific, although mesoderm and endoderm shared more than expected by chance. Ageing profiles were significantly more similar between tissues from the same germ layer than between tissues from different germ layers. Germ layer origin also explained 13.6% of the variation in tissue ageing profiles. Co-expression networks of ageing were organised differently in each germ layer, and 43% of enriched biological processes were specific to one germ layer. However, after grouping related processes, most functional themes were shared by all three, and genes shared between modules of different germ layers were enriched mainly for immune processes. Together, these results indicate that germ layer origin leaves a small but detectable imprint on transcriptomic ageing. However, tissue-specific and shared immune programmes are also prominent.

papers.title: An open long non-coding RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
papers.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play essential roles in transcriptional regulation and chromatin organization, yet predicting their functional properties from sequence remains challenging because informative signals span both local motifs and long-range base pairing across kilobase-scale transcripts. Current RNA foundation models are restricted to short sequences and existing lncRNA prediction models narrowly focus on isolated tasks, leaving a dedicated foundation model notably absent. Here we present LncRFM, a dedicated lncRNA foundation model, supported by the LncCorpus pretraining data and the LncBench evaluation suite, which stand for a systematic framework to decode lncRNAs. For foundation model pretraining, we develop a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder trained with a structure-guided masking strategy to effectively capture both local sequence patterns and long-range contexts. For pretraining data, we contribute over 9.6 million lncRNA sequences to assemble LncCorpus, a pretraining corpus of 24.7 million sequences. For benchmarking evaluation, we construct a comprehensive benchmark, LncBench, comprising 15 datasets and totaling over 1,010,000 sequences across 10 prediction tasks: six core lncRNA functional and annotation tasks and four structural and regulatory RNA assay tasks. Evaluated against seven RNA foundation models under a unified frozen-encoder protocol, our LncRFM achieves the state-of-the-art primary-metric scores on 11 of the 13 datasets that allow downstream adaptation. On two external generalization benchmarks evaluated without further adaptation, LncRFM matches the best structure-specialized baseline in F1 (0.141) and achieves the highest AUROC (0.962) on lncRNA contact prediction, while maintaining competitive cross-species coding-potential transfer (F1 of 0.374) under severe multi-kingdom domain shift. To benefit the scientific community, we make all datasets, source code, and pretrained models publicly available.

papers.title: EPIC2: integrating single-cell chromatin accessibility with human genetics to identify trait-relevant cell types
papers.abstract: Summary: EPIC2 is a computational and statistical framework for prioritizing trait-relevant cellular contexts by integrating genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics with single-cell chromatin accessibility data. It accounts for linkage disequilibrium when testing for association between GWAS association strength and cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility at both SNP and regulatory-peak resolutions. The resulting P-values are combined using the Cauchy combination test. Availability and Implementation: The core workflow is implemented in R, with source code, vignettes, and reproducible test data freely available at https://github.com/LingxuanZ/EPIC2. Supplementary Information: Supplementary material accompanies this preprint.

papers.title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research
papers.abstract: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.
